entry: Medical procedure for examining the interior of a hollow organ or body cavity with an endoscope. Unlike many other [[Medical imaging|medical imaging]] techniques, endoscopes are inserted directly into the organ. The procedure may be performed by a doctor or a surgeon, and the patient may be fully conscious or anesthetized. Most often the term refers to examination of the upper [[Gastrointestinal tract|gastrointestinal tract]], known as esophagogastroduodenoscopy. Endoscopy is used to investigate symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, difficulty swallowing and gastrointestinal bleeding. It is also used in diagnosis, most commonly by [[Biopsy|biopsy]], to check for conditions such as anemia, bleeding, inflammation and cancers of the digestive system. Treatments include cauterizing a bleeding vessel, widening a narrow [[Esophagus|esophagus]], clipping off a polyp and removing a foreign object. The term endoscope was first used on February 7, 1855, by engineer-optician Charles Chevalier. The self-illuminated endoscope was developed at Glasgow Royal Infirmary in Scotland in 1894/1895 by John Macintyre.

Industries involved in the production and sale of energy, including fuel extraction, manufacturing, refining and distribution. The industry is a crucial part of the infrastructure of society in almost all countries. It comprises the [[Fossil fuel|fossil fuel]] industries, including petroleum, [[Coal|coal]] and [[Natural gas|natural gas]] extraction and sales; the electrical power industry, including [[Electricity generation|electricity generation]] and distribution; the [[Nuclear power|nuclear power]] industry; the [[Renewable energy|renewable energy]] industry, including hydroelectric, wind and solar power; and the traditional collection and distribution of firewood for cooking and heating in poorer countries. The increasing use of energy since the [[Industrial Revolution|Industrial Revolution]] has brought serious problems, including global warming. Fossil fuels were the primary source of energy generation in most parts of the world and are a significant contributor to global warming and pollution. Many economies are investing in renewable and sustainable energy to limit global warming and reduce air pollution.

Discrete quantized value of energy of a bound [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanical]] system. Such a system can take only certain discrete energy values, unlike classical particles, which can have any amount of energy. The term is commonly used for the levels of electrons in [[Atom|atoms]], ions or [[Molecule|molecules]], which are bound by the [[Electric field|electric field]] of the nucleus. In atomic physics an [[Electron shell|electron shell]], or principal energy level, can be thought of as the orbit of one or more electrons around an atom's nucleus. The first shell can hold up to two electrons, the second up to eight and the third up to 18, and the nth shell can in principle hold up to 2n² electrons. An atom, ion or molecule at its lowest energy level is in the ground state; a higher level is excited. Measurement of an object's possible energy levels is called [[Spectroscopy|spectroscopy]]. The notion of energy levels was proposed in 1913 by Danish physicist [[Niels Bohr|Niels Bohr]].

Country of the [[United Kingdom|United Kingdom]], covering about 62% of the island of Great Britain (pop., 2021: 56,490,048). England shares land borders with [[Scotland|Scotland]] to the north and [[Wales|Wales]] to the west, and is surrounded by the North Sea, the English Channel, the Celtic Sea and the Irish Sea. The largest city is [[London|London]], with nine million inhabitants. The name derives from the Old English *Englaland*, meaning land of the Angles, a Germanic tribe. England became a unified state in the 10th century. The Kingdom of England ceased to be a separate sovereign state on May 1, 1707, when the Acts of Union formed the Kingdom of Great Britain. The Industrial Revolution began in 18th-century England, and English law served as the basis for the [[Common law|common law]] systems of many other countries. Terrain consists chiefly of low hills and plains, with uplands in the north and west, including the [[Lake District|Lake District]].

Arm of the [[Atlantic Ocean|Atlantic Ocean]] separating southern England from northern France. The Channel links to the southern part of the [[North Sea|North Sea]] through the [[Strait of Dover|Strait of Dover]] at its northeastern end. It is about 560 km long and varies in width from 240 km at its widest to 34 km at the Strait of Dover, covering some 75,000 sq km. It is the busiest shipping area in the world. The Channel helped the [[United Kingdom|United Kingdom]] become a naval superpower and served as a natural defense against invasions, such as in the [[Napoleonic Wars|Napoleonic Wars]] and the Second World War. Roman sources named it *Oceanus Britannicus*. The name English Channel was in common usage by the 18th century and in official use by the 19th century. The French name *la Manche* has been used since at least the 17th century.

Series of civil wars and political conflicts between Royalists and Parliamentarians in the [[Kingdom of England|Kingdom of England]], 1642–1651. It was part of the wider Wars of the Three Kingdoms, 1639–1653, which also involved [[Scotland|Scotland]], [[Ireland|Ireland]] and [[Wales|Wales]]. The First English Civil War was fought mainly over the balance of power between Parliament and Charles I, and ended in June 1646 with Royalist defeat and the king in custody. Disagreement among Parliamentarians over the political settlement followed. Royalist defeat in the 1648 Second English Civil War led to the execution of Charles I in January 1649 and the establishment of the Commonwealth of England. Concern over radicals in the New Model Army, including [[Oliver Cromwell|Oliver Cromwell]], had earlier led to an alliance between moderate Parliamentarians and Royalists. Parliamentarian victory at Worcester on September 3, 1651, ended the Anglo-Scottish war. The conflict popularized the terms Cavalier and Roundhead, and pamphlets of the 1640s are considered among the first examples of mass communication in English.

Latin-script alphabet of 26 letters, each with uppercase and lowercase forms, used to write [[Modern English|Modern English]]. It has five vowel letters, 19 consonant letters, and two letters, W and Y, that may function as either. Old English writing in the 5th century used the runic futhorc, and the Latin alphabet was adopted from the 7th century onward. By the 16th century the present set of 26 letters had largely stabilized. Diacritics are generally not used in native English words.

Literature written in the [[English language|English language]]. The earliest forms, called Old English, were brought to Great Britain by Anglo-Saxon settlers in the fifth century. The most famous work in Old English is *Beowulf*, which is set in Scandinavia but has achieved national epic status in England. After the [[Norman Conquest|Norman Conquest]] of 1066, French became the standard language of courts and polite society, and Middle English developed. [[Geoffrey Chaucer|Geoffrey Chaucer]], author of *The Canterbury Tales*, helped establish vernacular English as a literary language. Printing by [[Johannes Gutenberg|Johannes Gutenberg]], introduced in 1439, helped standardize the language. [[William Shakespeare|William Shakespeare]]'s plays have been translated into every primary living language and are performed more often than those of any other playwright. From 1907 to the present, writers from Great Britain, Ireland, the U.S. and former British colonies have received the Nobel Prize in Literature for works in English, more than in any other language.

Practice of incising a design into a hard, usually flat surface with a burin, a hardened steel tool. The result may be a decorated object, such as silver or gold, or an intaglio printing plate, usually of copper, for printing images on paper. Engraving is one of the oldest and most important techniques in [[Printmaking|printmaking]]. It developed in the 15th century in [[Germany|Germany]] and Italy and was historically used for artistic prints, maps, book illustrations and commercial reproductions. Photographic processes have replaced it in commercial applications, and etching has largely replaced it in printmaking. Traditional engraving is still practiced by goldsmiths, glass engravers and gunsmiths.

Sumerian high priestess of the moon god Nanna in the city-state of [[Ur|Ur]]. Her father was [[Sargon of Akkad|Sargon of Akkad]] (r. c. 2334 – c. 2279 BCE), founder of the [[Akkadian Empire|Akkadian Empire]], who likely appointed her to link his religion with native Sumerian religion. Enheduanna has been celebrated as the earliest known named author in world history. Several works in [[Sumerian language|Sumerian]] literature, such as the *Exaltation of Inanna*, feature her as first-person narrator, but scholars debate whether she composed them. The only surviving manuscripts were written by scribes six centuries after she lived. Her existence was rediscovered in 1927, when Sir Leonard Woolley excavated the Giparu at Ur and found an alabaster disk inscribed with her name. Her works have been studied as an early progenitor of classical rhetoric and have attracted attention in [[Feminism|feminism]].

Electromechanical [[Encryption|cipher]] device used in the early to mid-20th century to protect commercial, diplomatic and military communication. It was used extensively by [[Nazi Germany|Nazi Germany]] in [[World War II|World War II]], in all branches of the German military. Its rotors scrambled the 26 letters of the Latin alphabet, changing the electrical connections with each keypress. Poland first solved the machine in December 1932, and its sharing of the methods enabled the Allies to exploit Enigma-enciphered messages as a major source of intelligence. Many commentators say intelligence from decrypted Enigma and other ciphers shortened the war substantially.

[[Mesopotamia|Mesopotamian]] god of wisdom, crafts, fresh subterranean waters, magic and incantations. Also known as Ea in Akkadian, Enki was first worshipped in [[Sumer|Sumer]], where his main cult center was the city of Eridu. He was already a major deity at the time of the earliest written sources. His cult was particularly influential in the Ur III and Old Babylonian periods, when he formed a triad at the top of the pantheon with Anu and [[Enlil|Enlil]]. Enki/Ea became a major god in Hurrian religion and part of the Hittite pantheon in [[Anatolia|Anatolia]]. With the rise of [[Babylon|Babylon]] and its god Marduk, his cult lost importance, though he remained major in Babylonia. In myth he is a crafty counselor, and Mesopotamian tradition regarded him as the creator of humankind from [[Clay|clay]]. His primary symbols included the goat-fish, the ram-headed staff and the [[Turtle|turtle]].

Ancient [[Mesopotamia|Mesopotamian]] god of wind, air, earth and storms. First attested as the chief deity of the Sumerian pantheon, Enlil was later worshipped by the Akkadians, Babylonians, Assyrians and Hurrians. His main center of worship was the Ekur temple in Nippur, regarded as the link between heaven and earth. Enlil separates An (heaven) from Ki (earth), making the world habitable for humans. In the Babylonian flood myth he sends the flood to exterminate humanity, which has made too much noise and prevented him from sleeping. His cult declined after Nippur was sacked by the [[Elam|Elamites]] in 1230 BC, and the Babylonian god Marduk eventually supplanted him as chief god of the pantheon. Enlil also features in the myth of Enlil and Ninlil and in myths involving his son Ninurta.

British politician and classical scholar. Powell was Conservative Member of Parliament for Wolverhampton South West from 1950 to 1974 and Minister of Health from 1960 to 1963. His 1968 "Rivers of Blood" speech criticized immigration to Britain, especially the influx from the [[Commonwealth of Nations|Commonwealth of Nations]]. Edward Heath dismissed him from the Shadow Cabinet the day after the speech, and several polls suggested that between 67 and 82 percent of the British population agreed with him. From 1974 to 1987 he was Ulster Unionist MP for South Down in [[Northern Ireland|Northern Ireland]].

[[Boeing B-29 Superfortress|Boeing B-29 Superfortress]] bomber, the first aircraft to drop an atomic bomb in warfare. Named after Enola Gay Tibbets, mother of its pilot, Colonel Paul Tibbets, it dropped the bomb code-named Little Boy on [[Hiroshima|Hiroshima]] on August 6, 1945, destroying about three-quarters of the city. For the second nuclear attack it served as weather reconnaissance aircraft for the primary target, Kokura, and [[Nagasaki|Nagasaki]] was bombed instead because of clouds and drifting smoke. After the war it was transferred to the [[Smithsonian Institution|Smithsonian Institution]]. The restored bomber has been displayed at the National Air and Space Museum's Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center since 2003.

Italian operatic tenor and the first international recording star. Caruso was born in [[Naples|Naples]], the third of seven children of parents from [[Campania|Campania]]. He worked as a street singer and at his father's factory before his professional stage debut in Naples in 1895. In 1900 he was given a contract to sing at La Scala. His American debut came at the Metropolitan Opera in 1903, as the Duke of Mantua in [[Giuseppe Verdi|Giuseppe Verdi]]'s *Rigoletto*, and he sang nearly every opening night there over 18 years. Caruso made around 250 commercially released recordings between 1902 and 1920. His 1904 recording of "Vesti la giubba" from *Pagliacci* sold more than one million copies.

Italian-American physicist and creator of the world's first artificial nuclear reactor, Chicago Pile-1. He won the 1938 Nobel Prize in Physics for demonstrations of new radioactive elements produced by neutron irradiation, though these were later shown to be [[Nuclear fission|nuclear fission]] products. He left Italy in 1938 to escape new racial laws that affected his Jewish wife, Laura Capon, and emigrated to the United States. Fermi led the team at the [[University of Chicago|University of Chicago]] that built Chicago Pile-1, which went critical on December 2, 1942, demonstrating the first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction. He was present at the [[Trinity (nuclear test)|Trinity test]] on July 16, 1945, and later opposed development of the hydrogen bomb on moral and technical grounds. His theoretical work included the naming of the [[Neutrino|neutrino]], a particle postulated by Wolfgang Pauli, and the [[Weak interaction|weak interaction]] theory. He also worked on the [[Manhattan Project|Manhattan Project]] during World War II.

Spanish singer and songwriter called the King of Latin Pop. Iglesias was born in [[Madrid|Madrid]] to singer [[Julio Iglesias|Julio Iglesias]] and spent much of his childhood in [[Miami|Miami]]. He began recording in the mid-1990s for the Mexican label Fonovisa, and by the turn of the millennium had crossed over into the English-language market. He signed a multi-album deal with [[Universal Music Group|Universal Music Group]]. His sales are estimated at over 100 million albums worldwide. He holds the record for the most number-one songs on Billboard's Hot Latin Songs chart, with 27.

Thermodynamic quantity equal to the sum of a system's [[Internal energy|internal energy]] and the product of its pressure and volume. Enthalpy is a state function, depending only on the final configuration of internal energy, pressure and volume rather than on the path taken. A change in enthalpy is the preferred expression for measurements at constant pressure, which Earth's atmosphere conveniently provides. When no matter is transferred and no work is done, the enthalpy change at constant pressure equals the energy exchanged as [[Heat|heat]]. The SI unit is the [[Joule|joule]]; the [[Calorie|calorie]] and the British thermal unit are historical units. The standard enthalpy of reaction is the enthalpy change when reactants in their standard states change to products in their standard states, usually at 1 [[Bar (unit)|bar]] and 298 K. Enthalpy change is positive for endothermic processes and negative for exothermic ones. The word derives from the Greek *enthalpein*, meaning to heat.

Thermodynamic state variable that quantifies the distribution of accessible microstates in a system. Entropy is central to the [[Second law of thermodynamics|second law of thermodynamics]], which states that the entropy of an isolated system left to spontaneous evolution cannot decrease, so isolated systems evolve toward equilibrium, where entropy is highest. Rudolf Clausius defined it in 1865 as the quotient of an infinitesimal amount of [[Heat|heat]] to the instantaneous temperature. [[Ludwig Boltzmann|Ludwig Boltzmann]] explained entropy as a measure of the number of possible microscopic arrangements of atoms and molecules that comply with a system's macroscopic condition, in a simple logarithmic law with the [[Boltzmann constant|Boltzmann constant]]. The concept has applications in [[Cosmology|cosmology]], [[Economics|economics]] and [[Information theory|information theory]].

Measure of the average uncertainty in the possible outcomes of a [[Random variable|random variable]]. Introduced by [[Claude Shannon|Claude Shannon]] in his 1948 paper "A Mathematical Theory of Communication", it is also called Shannon entropy. Base 2 gives units of bits. Shannon proved that entropy sets an absolute limit on how well data from a source can be losslessly compressed. The measure is formally identical to Gibbs's formula for entropy in statistical thermodynamics, and it applies in [[Machine learning|machine learning]] and [[Combinatorics|combinatorics]].

Capital city of Enugu State in southeastern [[Nigeria|Nigeria]] (pop., 2024 est.: 876,000). The name is derived from two [[Igbo language|Igbo]] words meaning hilltop, reflecting the city's hilly geography. The first settlement was the Nike village of Ogui, whose people acquired much of their land through slave raiding in the era of the [[Atlantic slave trade|Atlantic slave trade]]. The Aro Confederacy (1690–1901) controlled slave trading in the area. Coal was found under the village of Enugwu Ngwo by 1909, and by 1913 it was confirmed in commercially viable quantities. The area acquired township status in 1917 as Enugwu-Ngwo and was renamed Enugu in 1928. Industrialization brought settlements around the colliery and the Eastern Line railway built by the British.

Turkish military officer, revolutionary and convicted war criminal. Enver served as Ottoman Minister of War from 1914 to 1918 and was one of the Three Pashas who ruled the [[Ottoman Empire|Ottoman Empire]] during [[World War I|World War I]], along with Talaat and Djemal. He was a key leader of the 1908 Young Turk Revolution and became war minister after the 1913 coup. He initiated the alliance with Germany and was instrumental in the Ottoman entry into the war. After a defeat at the Battle of Sarikamish, he blamed Armenians for his defeat. An Ottoman military tribunal convicted him in absentia for bringing the empire into the war and for organizing massacres against Greeks and Armenians. He led the Basmachi Revolt against the [[Bolsheviks|Bolsheviks]] in Central Asia before he was killed in combat.

Scientific study of the chemical and biochemical phenomena that occur in natural places. The field studies the sources, reactions, transport, effects and fates of chemical species in air, soil and water, and the effects of human and biological activity on them. It is interdisciplinary, drawing on atmospheric, aquatic and soil chemistry, and relies heavily on [[Analytical chemistry|analytical chemistry]]. Understanding how the uncontaminated environment works comes first. A contaminant is a substance present in nature at a level higher than fixed levels, and is often used interchangeably with pollutant. Typical pollutants include heavy metals from industry, [[Pesticide|pesticides]], nutrients leaching from farmland into waterways, and urban runoff of [[Gasoline|gasoline]] and [[Sediment|sediment]]. Quantitative analysis uses methods such as atomic spectroscopy and [[Mass spectrometry|mass spectrometry]], with [[Chromatography|chromatography]] used for organic compounds.

Broad philosophy, ideology and [[Social movement|social movement]] supporting life, habitats and surroundings. Environmentalism advocates the preservation, restoration and improvement of the natural environment and of earth system elements such as the [[Climate|climate]]. Concepts such as environmental ethics, [[Biodiversity|biodiversity]], [[Ecology|ecology]] and the biophilia hypothesis figure prominently. It seeks to balance relations between humans and the natural systems on which they depend, with a proper degree of [[Sustainability|sustainability]]. Its approaches include the environmental conservation movement and free market environmentalism. The movement emerged from 19th-century conservation initiatives, such as the U.S. [[National park|national parks]] inspired by [[John Muir|John Muir]], and expanded in the mid-20th century amid concern over pollution. Debate continues over the economic costs of stringent environmental policies. Anti-environmentalism opposes the movement, holding that the Earth is less fragile than environmentalists maintain.
